subject: chem
title: Chemical Bonding
subtitle: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding; shapes of molecules; intermolecular forces.
concept: Bonding type depends on electronegativity difference: large difference → ionic; small/zero → covalent; metal atoms → metallic.
VSEPR theory predicts molecular shape based on electron pairs (bonding and lone pairs) repelling each other to maximum separation.
Intermolecular forces (van der Waals, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding) determine physical properties such as boiling point and solubility.

notes.heading: Types of Chemical Bond
items: Ionic bonds form by electron transfer between atoms of very different electronegativity — a metal loses electrons to form a cation; a non-metal gains them to form an anion. The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions is the ionic bond. Ionic compounds have high melting points, conduct electricity when molten or dissolved, and form giant lattice structures.

Covalent bonds form by sharing a pair of electrons between atoms of similar electronegativity. A single bond is one shared pair (σ bond); a double bond is two pairs (1 σ + 1 π); a triple bond is three pairs (1 σ + 2 π). A dative (coordinate) bond forms when both electrons come from the same atom (e.g. the N–H⁺ bond in NH₄⁺).

Metallic bonds result from the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and delocalised electrons. High melting points (especially for small, highly charged ions), good electrical/thermal conductors, malleable and ductile.

notes.heading: Shapes of Molecules — VSEPR Theory
items: Electron pairs (bonding pairs and lone pairs) repel each other and adopt positions that maximise separation. Lone pairs exert greater repulsion than bonding pairs, compressing bond angles.

2 pairs: linear (180°). 3 BP + 0 LP: trigonal planar (120°). 4 BP + 0 LP: tetrahedral (109.5°). 3 BP + 1 LP: pyramidal (~107°). 2 BP + 2 LP: bent (~104.5°). 5 BP: trigonal bipyramidal. 6 BP: octahedral (90°).

notes.heading: Electronegativity and Polarity
items: Electronegativity increases across a period and up a group. A polar bond has δ+ and δ− ends due to unequal electron sharing. A molecule is polar only if the bond dipoles do not cancel — CO₂ is linear so the two C=O dipoles cancel (non-polar); H₂O is bent so they do not (polar).

notes.heading: Intermolecular Forces
items: Instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (id-id) forces (van der Waals/London forces) exist in ALL molecules. They arise from temporary uneven electron distribution; their strength increases with molecular mass and surface area.
Permanent dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules — weaker than hydrogen bonds but stronger than id-id forces of similar-sized non-polar molecules.

Hydrogen bonds form when H is bonded to N, O or F and interacts with a lone pair on another N, O or F atom. They explain: the anomalously high boiling point of H₂O, HF, and NH₃; the low density of ice (open hexagonal lattice); DNA double helix stability; protein secondary and tertiary structure.

definitions.body: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
A covalent bond in which both electrons come from the same atom, e.g. NH₄⁺ formation.
The ability of an atom to attract the bonding electron pair towards itself.
An intermolecular force between a δ+ hydrogen on N–H, O–H or F–H and a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule.

workedExamples.q: Predict the shape and bond angle of SF₄.

steps.text: S has 6 valence e⁻. 4 bonding pairs with F = 8e used. Remaining: 6−4 = 2e → 1 lone pair.
4 BP + 1 LP = 5 electron pairs → based on trigonal bipyramidal.
Lone pair occupies equatorial position (more space). Shape: see-saw. Bond angles: ~117° (equatorial) and ~87° (axial).

workedExamples.q: Explain why the boiling point of H₂O is much higher than H₂S.

steps.text: H₂O forms hydrogen bonds (O–H···O); H₂S only has permanent dipole–dipole and id-id forces.
Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than dipole–dipole forces.
More energy is required to overcome hydrogen bonds in H₂O, giving it a much higher BP despite lower molecular mass.

mistakes: Forgetting that lone pairs count as electron pairs in VSEPR but are not shown in the shape name.
Stating that CO₂ is polar because each C=O bond is polar — the bonds cancel in the linear molecule.
Confusing bond polarity (property of a bond) with molecular polarity (property of the whole molecule).
tips: Draw the Lewis structure first, then apply VSEPR — always show lone pairs on the central atom.
Hydrogen bonding requires: H bonded to N, O or F, AND a lone pair on N, O or F on another molecule — state both.
For exam questions on intermolecular forces, always say 'instantaneous dipole–induced dipole' (not just 'van der Waals') for full marks.

flashcards.q: What bond angle is found in a tetrahedral molecule with no lone pairs?
Why does NH₃ have a bond angle of ~107° rather than 109.5°?
flashcards.a: The lone pair on N repels the bonding pairs more than bonding pairs repel each other, compressing the angle.

flashcards.q: What condition is needed to form a hydrogen bond?
flashcards.a: H must be bonded to N, O or F; and the H must interact with a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule.

flashcards.q: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?
flashcards.a: In ice, hydrogen bonds lock water molecules into an open hexagonal lattice, which is less dense than the more disordered liquid.
A covalent bond where both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom.

flashcards.q: What shape is BF₃ and why?
flashcards.a: Trigonal planar (120°) — 3 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs around B.

questions.q: What is the shape of PCl₅?
questions.exp: P has 5 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs → trigonal bipyramidal.

questions.q: Which molecule has the highest boiling point?
questions.exp: NH₃ forms hydrogen bonds (N–H···N); the others only have id-id forces.

questions.q: Which of these is a polar molecule?
questions.exp: CHCl₃ is tetrahedral but the three C–Cl dipoles do not cancel the C–H dipole.

questions.q: What type of bonding explains why metals conduct electricity?
questions.exp: Delocalised electrons in metallic bonding are free to carry charge.

questions.q: In which molecule does the central atom have two lone pairs?
questions.exp: O has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs → bent shape, ~104.5°.
